title: RBAC, Audit Logging, Data Residency & Compliance Evidence Playbook
author: Aisha Patel
content:
Overview:

This playbook consolidates Redwood Inference's operational guidance for role-based access control (RBAC) and authentication, audit logging strategy, data residency and retention policies, secure SDLC controls, incident response procedures for security events, compliance evidence workflows, and the risk & exceptions process. It is intended for engineering leads, platform engineers, compliance owners, security reviewers, and auditors.

Scope:
- Applies to all Redwood-managed control plane services, customer-facing APIs, internal admin consoles, and private deployment support stacks.
- Covers production, staging, and dedicated customer environments unless explicitly scoped otherwise by a policy exception.

Owners & Contacts:
- Policy owner: Security (security@redwood.ai)
- RBAC primary: Platform IAM team (platform-iam@redwood.ai)
- Audit logging & retention: Observability team (observability@redwood.ai)
- SDLC controls: Eng DX / Security (eng-dx@redwood.ai, security@redwood.ai)
- Incident response owner: SRE & Security on-call (pager duty: #sec-sre)

1) RBAC & Authentication 

Goal: Enforce least privilege across services and infrastructure while preserving developer velocity. 

Model overview:
- Principal types: human users (SSO via Okta), service principals (short-lived service tokens), CI identities (GitHub Actions), and cross-account roles for Dedicated/Private deployments.
- Role types: Viewer (read-only), Operator (deploy/run but no customer data access), Admin (config + infra), Security (audit + policy), Customer-Admin (customer-scoped in Dedicated/Private).
- Policy format: All roles are defined in the central IAM catalog (repo: infra/iam/roles) as JSON policy documents. Changes require PR, code review, and approval from the IAM owner.

Minimum requirements:
1. All human access must use SSO (Okta) with MFA enforced.
2. No long-lived static API keys for services in production. Use short-lived tokens (Vault/OIDC).
3. Privileged roles require approval via Access Request workflow (Jira ticket + manager + security).

Example service principal policy (example):
```json
{
  "version": "2024-01-01",
  "statement": [
    {"effect": "allow", "action": ["runtime:InvokeModel"], "resource": ["arn:rw:inference:service:prod:*/models/*"]},
    {"effect": "deny", "action": ["data:ReadCustomerPII"], "resource": ["arn:rw:data:customers:*:*"]}
  ]
}
```

Role lifecycle:
- Creation: submit PR against infra/iam/roles with role name, scope, and justification.
- Review: platform-iam reviews within 5 business days.
- Provisioning: automated by iam-controller; errors are reported to #iam-alerts.
- Decommission: Roles must include an expiry date; annual review required.

2) Audit Logging

Objective: Centralize and retain tamper-evident logs to support investigations and compliance evidence requests.

What to log (minimum):
- Authentication events: SSO logins, MFA failures, token issuance/refresh.
- Authorization decisions: role grants, policy evaluations, access request approvals/denials.
- Privileged actions: schema changes, secret updates, IAM policy changes, canary rollouts to production.
- Data exfiltration indicators: large bulk export jobs, unusual download events.
- Platform runtime events: model deploys, fallback events, scaling actions that impact isolation.

Log pipeline and storage:
- Log sources: application (structured JSON logs), infrastructure (CloudTrail/Audit Logs), network (flow logs), and host agents (OS auditd).
- Aggregation: Fluentd -> Kafka -> Splunk/Elasticsearch (primary analytics) -> S3 cold archive.
- Retention tiers: 90 days hot in Splunk for search, 7 years archived in S3 (see retention table).
- Integrity: daily signed manifests on S3; retention bucket enforces object lock for regulatory buckets.

Alerting thresholds (examples):
- >5 failed MFA attempts for a single user within 1 hour: P2 alert to #sec-sre.
- Unexpected IAM policy change in prod: P1 alert + auto page to on-call.

3) Data Residency & Retention

Purpose: Ensure customer and system data are stored according to contractual obligations and regional regulations.

Retention policy (summary table):
- Customer request payloads: region-matched storage; retention: default 30 days (configurable per-customer: 7/30/90/365).
- Audit logs (platform): retention hot 90 days; archive 7 years.
- Access logs (admin console): retention 1 year.
- Compliance evidence artifacts: retention 7 years.
- Backups (config + state): retention 90 days by default; critical-prod backups 1 year.

Table (data type | default region policy | default retention):
- Customer data | region of record (EU/US/APAC) | 30 days (customer-configurable)
- Audit logs | Global primary region + archive | 90 days / 7 years archive
- Admin access logs | Global | 1 year
- Compliance evidence | Secure evidence bucket (us-west-2) | 7 years

Geofencing:
- Deployments serving EU-only customers must use EU regions for both compute and persistent storage (examples: eu-west-1 for compute, s3.eu-west-1 for object storage).
- Cross-region failover allowed only with explicit customer consent and documented mitigation.

Data deletion workflow (customer-requested):
1. Customer submits deletion request (support ticket) referencing deployment and dataset.
2. Support validates identity and obtains approval from Data Privacy team.
3. Data is queued for deletion, snapshot taken for audit reference (metadata only), deletion executed, and verification recorded in the audit log.
4. Evidence of deletion stored in compliance-evidence-bucket with ticket ID and timestamp.

4) Secure SDLC Controls

Goal: Prevent vulnerabilities from entering production and ensure traceable evidence of security gates.

Gates & tooling:
- Source control: GitHub with branch protection; all production changes require PR with two reviewers (at least one security/infra reviewer for infra/config changes).
- Static Analysis: SAST on PRs (Semgrep + custom rules).
- Secrets scanning: Repo scanning (git-secrets) and pre-commit hooks; CI rejects commits with secrets.
- Dependency management: Dependabot for automated update PRs; high-severity CVEs require one security reviewer and expedited patching (72-hour SLA).
- Container/image scanning: CI runs Clair/Trivy; builds failing critical vulnerabilities blocked from release.
- Runtime protections: Runtime RBAC checks, network policies, and mutating admission controllers in k8s clusters.

Release checklist (must-pass items):
1. PR approved and merged with required reviewers.
2. CI green and SAST/DAST scans passed or documented risk accepted.
3. Secrets check passed and config reviewed.
4. Canary deployment plan and rollback procedure documented.
5. Monitoring/alerting for the release validated.

Evidence capture:
- Every release must attach CI run artifacts (build ID, SAST/DAST reports), PR diff, approver list, and canary run metrics to the release ticket. These artifacts are copied to the compliance evidence store at release time.

5) Incident Response — Security Procedures

Purpose: Provide clear steps for security incident detection, triage, containment, eradication, and postmortem with evidence preservation.

High-level process (numbered):
1. Detection & classification: Security/Ops detects event via alerts, IDS, or reports. Classify severity: P1 (data compromise / service compromise), P2 (privilege escalation attempt), P3 (non-sensitive operational issue).
2. Triage: Owner assigned (on-call sec or SRE). Collect initial scope: affected services, time window, and impacted customers.
3. Containment: Short-term (isolate host, revoke tokens) and long-term (apply hotfix, block IP ranges).
4. Evidence preservation: Snapshot hosts, export logs for the incident window, preserve relevant S3 objects with object-lock enabled.
5. Eradication & recovery: Patch, rotate credentials, validate with smoke tests and replayed requests.
6. Notification: Follow internal notification matrix and customer notification policy (see below).
7. Post-incident review: Produce an incident report within 7 days, include technical root cause analysis, timeline, impact, and remediation plan.

Forensic checklist (initial):
- Timestamped log export (authentication, authorization, and app logs)
- Host memory snapshot (if applicable)
- Network captures (pcap) for affected windows
- List of active secrets/tokens and rotation status

Customer notification thresholds:
- P1 affecting customer data: notify affected customers within 72 hours, coordinated with legal and comms.
- P2 that materially impacts availability: notify customers within 7 days with mitigation plan.

6) Compliance Evidence Workflows

Objective: Produce auditable artifacts to satisfy SOC2/ISO/GDPR requests and internal audits.

Evidence types and owners (examples):
- IAM policy change history: Owner = Platform IAM; artifact = commit history & Splunk audit log export.
- Role assignments: Owner = Platform IAM; artifact = access-request tickets + provisioning logs.
- SAST/DAST reports: Owner = Eng DX; artifact = CI reports stored at artifacts/reports/<build-id>.
- Pen test reports: Owner = Security; artifact = engagement report, remediation evidence, and retest results.
- Incident reports: Owner = SRE/Security; artifact = incident ticket, timeline, preserved logs.

Evidence request handling (process):
1. Request received (internal audit or external auditor) via compliance@redwood.ai ticket.
2. Compliance owner maps controls -> artifacts and assigns collection tasks.
3. Owners collect artifacts and upload to the evidence vault (S3 bucket with restricted access and MFA delete).
4. Compliance reviews, validates, and marks request closed.
5. External auditors receive a read-only bundle (time-limited signed URL) and an index file describing artifact provenance.

Artifact provenance must include:
- Source system, extraction query, extraction timestamp, extractor name, and verification checksum.

7) Risk & Exceptions Process

When a control cannot be implemented as written, teams may request a temporary exception. Exceptions are time-boxed and reviewed.

Exception request template (fields):
- Policy or control ID
- Justification and business impact
- Proposed compensating controls
- Risk owner and approver
- Expiry date (max 90 days without extension)

Approval flow:
1. Submit exception via Jira template (project: SEC-EXCEPTIONS).
2. Security reviews and either Approves, Approves with conditions, or Denies within 7 business days.
3. Approved exceptions are tracked in the Exceptions register and require evidence of compensating controls.

Periodic review:
- All exceptions are reviewed at least monthly by Security; long-running exceptions (>90 days) require exec-level sponsor and quarterly risk re-approval.

Appendices:
A. Useful commands / snippets:
- Export IAM audit logs (example CLI):
  aws cloudtrail lookup-events --lookup-attributes AttributeKey=EventName,AttributeValue=PutRolePolicy --start-time 2026-01-01T00:00:00Z --end-time 2026-04-20T23:59:59Z > iam-events.json

- Upload evidence to secure bucket (example):
  aws s3 cp sast-report.json s3://redwood-compliance-evidence/prod/<ticket-id>/ --server-side-encryption aws:kms

B. Evidence storage locations:
- Compliance evidence bucket: s3://redwood-compliance-evidence (restricted, MFA delete, object-lock enabled)
- Hot analytics (Splunk): index=redwood_audit_prod

C. Related policies and docs:
- security-and-compliance-controlbook (see related_pages)
- incident-response-runbook (confluence/ oncall-and-incident-response)

D. Frequently asked questions:
- "How long do we keep customer request payloads?" Default 30 days unless customer contract specifies otherwise.
- "Who can approve role escalations?" Manager + Security must approve for Prod-level roles.

Revision history:
- 2026-04-20: Created by Aisha Patel (initial published version).
- 2026-11-12: Added SSO MFA enforcement and updated evidence storage requirements.
- 2027-02-10: Clarified exception expiry and added archive object-lock guidance.

End of playbook.
